text:
Shanty Town
2023 • Nigerian Crime Drama • 6 Episodes
Score: 6.73
Crime, Drama
What It Feels Like to Watch
Shanty Town is a Nigerian crime drama that plunges into Lagos's underground—a world of gangsters, corrupt politicians, and women caught in systems of exploitation. The series follows multiple characters whose lives intersect through violence and survival: a fixer looking for a way out, prostitutes planning escape, a politician whose ambitions require dirty work, and the gang leader who controls all of it. It's a familiar crime-drama structure executed with local specificity that makes it feel fresh.
The show's strongest asset is its setting. Lagos comes alive not as exotic backdrop but as a character with its own rules and rhythms. The shanty town itself—the cramped spaces, the precarious economics, the social networks that sustain and trap people—is rendered with eye for detail that suggests lived experience rather than research. The production design communicates poverty and density without tourism, showing why people stay even when they dream of leaving.
Where Shanty Town struggles is in balancing its multiple storylines within six episodes. Characters are introduced and dispatched with a speed that doesn't allow for development, and some arcs feel truncated by the constraint of the limited series format. The violence is frequent and explicit, which serves the show's themes but can feel relentless. What distinguishes it from countless other crime dramas is the Nigerian context—the particular forms that corruption takes, the role of traditional authority alongside modern power, the women whose options are constrained in ways that the show treats seriously rather than exploitatively.
Why It Ranks Here
Shanty Town earns its position through atmosphere and specificity rather than narrative innovation. It's a competent crime thriller elevated by its setting and the freshness of Nigerian cinema for international audiences. The score reflects solid execution within a familiar genre framework.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7/10)
The cast conveys the hardness required by the material without losing humanity. The gang leader is genuinely menacing without becoming cartoonish; the women attempting escape have agency despite their constrained circumstances. The performances are physical in a way that matches the environment—bodies that have survived, faces that have seen too much. Chidi Mokeme as Scar is particularly effective, communicating threat through stillness.
World Building (7/10)
Lagos's criminal underworld is rendered with specificity that suggests authenticity. The relationship between street-level operations and political power feels true to the Nigerian context, where these worlds overlap rather than remain separate. The shanty town itself is a fully realized environment—claustrophobic, dangerous, but also home to the people who live there.
Cinematography (6.5/10)
The visual style leans into darkness—many scenes are lit by single sources, creating deep shadows that match the moral terrain. The camera moves through crowded spaces with the density of real Lagos streets. There's an effective contrast between the gritty shanty town and the cleaner spaces of political power, highlighting class division visually.
Visual Spectacle (5/10)
The spectacle here is violence—shootouts, beatings, scenes of exploitation rendered unsparingly. It's not action cinema; the violence is ugly rather than thrilling, which is appropriate to the material but limits the visual pleasure. The production design of the shanty town itself provides the primary visual interest.
Conceptual Depth (6/10)
The show engages with systems of exploitation—the way poverty creates vulnerability, how power protects itself, the limited options available to women in particular circumstances. These themes are present but not explored with depth; the narrative momentum doesn't pause for analysis. The Nigerian setting adds specificity but doesn't change the underlying crime-drama framework.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Multiple storylines converge over six episodes with efficiency. The limited episode count forces focus—there's no room for filler. Each episode advances at least one character arc toward its destination. The momentum is sometimes too aggressive, sacrificing character development for plot progression.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
The finale resolves some arcs definitively while leaving others open, suggesting either sequel ambitions or narrative uncertainty. The deaths feel earned, the escapes feel possible, the political machinations feel ongoing. It's a conclusion that satisfies without completing, which fits the show's themes about systems that persist beyond individual stories.

16th-century England. Matthew Shardlake is a lawyer with a curved spine, working for Thomas Cromwell, investigating monasteries scheduled for dissolution. C.J. Sansom's novels adapted: Tudor politics, murder, and a detective who's an outsider in his own time. Arthur Hughes is Shardlake—disabled, brilliant, determined. Sean Bean is Cromwell, the dangerous patron. Historical mystery as Tudor noir.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8/10)
Arthur Hughes embodies Shardlake: the physical difference that makes him an outsider, the intelligence that makes him essential, the moral compass that conflicts with Cromwell's ruthlessness. Sean Bean's Cromwell is understated menace. The supporting cast creates the monastery world—monks with secrets, politics with stakes.
World Building (8/10)
Henrician England: the fear of Cromwell, the destruction of monasteries, the religious revolution that made enemies of old allies. The monastery of Scarnsea is specific—its monks, its history, its secrets. The world is historical mystery at its best: accurate, atmospheric, plot-relevant.
Cinematography (7/10)
Period production with appropriate gloom: candlelit corridors, monastery cloisters, Tudor architecture. The style serves the mystery—shadows for secrets, confined spaces for claustrophobia. The visual language is competent without being distinctive.
Visual Spectacle (5/10)
Tudor England rendered: the monastery, the travel, the execution sites. The spectacle is period atmosphere rather than action. The production value is visible; the budget is not blockbuster.
Conceptual Density (7/10)
Power, disability, faith vs. politics. Shardlake's physical difference is treated seriously—Tudor attitudes to disability, his resilience, his awareness of being judged. The Reformation provides context: monasteries being destroyed, a king remaking religion. History with depth.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Four-episode mystery: a murder at Scarnsea, Cromwell's demands, Shardlake's investigation. The structure is classic whodunit in period dress. The stakes are political—failure means Cromwell's displeasure, which means death. The pacing is appropriate; the mystery is satisfying.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
Miniseries adapting one novel. The mystery resolves; the larger story (Shardlake's career) could continue if renewed. Sansom wrote multiple novels; the adaptation potential exists. Currently complete as a single story.

text:
Sharp Objects
2018 • Psychological Thriller | 8 Episodes
Score: 8.35
Thriller, Drama, Mystery
What It Feels Like to Watch
Sharp Objects is a limited series about Camille Preaker, a journalist who returns to her Missouri hometown to investigate the murder of a young girl and begins confronting her own traumatic history. Amy Adams plays Camille as someone barely holding herself together, a woman whose self-destruction through alcohol and scarification is the only way she can feel anything. The show is based on Gillian Flynn's novel and adapted by Marti Noxon and Jean-Marc Vallée.
Jean-Marc Vallée's direction creates atmosphere through visual fragmentation—quick cuts, flashbacks that bleed into present, Camille's memories disturbing reality without warning. The show is built on mood: Southern Gothic heat, the decay of a town that was never prosperous, the secrets that everyone knows but no one discusses. Patricia Clarkson's Adora, Camille's mother, is a piece of work—a woman whose Southern charm covers absolute narcissism, whose love is weaponized, whose own damage is passed down through generations.
What distinguishes Sharp Objects is its complete commitment to Camille's damaged psychology. The mystery is never less than gripping, but it's secondary to the portrait of a woman carrying wounds that never healed. The show's formal restlessness—its fragmented structure, its refusal of conventional pacing—mirrors Camille's consciousness. Eliza Scanlen plays Camille's half-sister Amma with dangerous energy that keeps you uncertain how to read her. The ending provides revelation that reframes everything without cheating; each clue was present, just obscured by the fever dream atmosphere. This is Southern Gothic at its most suffocating.
Why It Ranks Here
Sharp Objects earns its ranking through Amy Adams's devastating performance, Jean-Marc Vallée's atmospheric direction, and a mystery that serves psychological depth. The score reflects limited series television at its most committed.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (9/10)
Amy Adams' Camille is a performance of damage barely contained—her physical stillness, her eyes that see everything without reacting appropriately. Patricia Clarkson creates a mother-who-was-never-mothering with terrifying charm. Eliza Scanlen's Amma is unreadable in ways that serve the mystery. The casting is perfect, the performances committed.
World Building (8/10)
Wind Gap, Missouri is Southern Gothic rendered in sweat and decay. The town's class hierarchy, the gossip network, the way everyone knows everyone else's business but pretends not to. The world is claustrophobic and specific.
Cinematography (8.5/10)
Vallée's direction fragments time and perception—flashbacks interrupt present, memories color perception. The visual style serves Camille's psychology without being showy. The direction is the show's central achievement.
Visual Spectacle (4/10)
The spectacle is in the final episode's revelation, in atmospheric decay, in Camille's physicality. No effects, no formal spectacle. The visual interest is in fragmentation and atmosphere.
Conceptual Depth (7.5/10)
The show explores intergenerational trauma, the ways women harm each other through love, the legacy of abuse passed down as normalcy. The mystery is secondary to the portrait of damage. The themes emerge from character and atmosphere.
Narrative Drive (7.5/10)
The murder investigation provides momentum, but the show is equally interested in Camille's psychology and her fractured relationship with her family. The pacing is deliberate—some viewers found it slow; others found it appropriate to mood. Eight episodes is the right length.
Narrative Path & Resolution (8.5/10)
The finale provides revelation that changes how you see everything that came before without cheating—every clue was present. The resolution of the mystery is stunning; the resolution of Camille's story is appropriately open. This is how limited series should end.

text:
Sherlock (S1-3)
2010 - 2014 • BBC • 9 Episodes
Score: 7.70
Mystery, Crime Drama
What It Feels Like
Sherlock Holmes in contemporary London. Texting instead of telegrams, nicotine patches instead of pipes, consulting detective as profession. Benedict Cumberbatch is the sociopath we can't look away from; Martin Freeman is the moral center we need. Steven Moffat and Mark Gatiss update Conan Doyle with reverence and invention—each episode a feature-length puzzle box. The first three seasons were lightning: sharp, confident, revolutionary. Then it got pleased with itself.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (9/10)
Cumberbatch's Sherlock is iconic: the speed, the disdain, the occasional flashes of something almost human. Freeman's Watson is the necessary anchor—wounded, loyal, the window through which we view genius. Andrew Scott's Moriarty is chaos incarnate. The supporting cast—Una Stubbs, Rupert Graves, Louise Brealey—provides dimension. The chemistry between the leads defines the show.
World Building (7/10)
Modern London as playground: Baker Street, the Diogenes Club, the British government's surveillance apparatus. The show creates a credible world where a consulting detective might exist—police who tolerate him, criminals who challenge him, a brother who controls him. The world is sufficient, though secondary to the puzzles.
Cinematography (8/10)
Visual storytelling as deduction: text messages floating on screen, thought processes rendered visible, timelines compressed into split-seconds. The technique was revolutionary when introduced; it influenced everything after. The cinematography makes thinking cinematic—watching someone reason becomes as dramatic as watching them fight.
Visual Spectacle (6/10)
The spectacle is intellectual: deductions that feel like magic, puzzles solved at speed. The production is BBC-budget elevated—London looks good, the Baker Street flat is perfect. Action sequences are staged competently. The spectacle serves the story rather than overwhelming it.
Conceptual Density (7/10)
Updating Holmes to the present raises questions: what does genius look like in an information age? What does friendship mean when one party can't reciprocate emotion? The show explores these without belaboring. The cases are variations on Conan Doyle; the innovation is context, not concept.
Narrative Drive (8/10)
Seasons 1-3 are propulsive: each 90-minute episode is a complete mystery with serialized character development. The cliffhangers are legendary—Sherlock's death, his return, the apparent return of Moriarty. The drive is constant. Seasons 4 (excluded from this ranking) lost momentum; the first three seasons maintain it.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
Seasons 1-3 tell a complete arc: meeting, partnering, apparent death, return. But the show continued into season 4, which many consider a decline. The exclusion of season 4 protects the ranking—this is Sherlock at its peak, before self-indulgence overwhelmed invention. Incomplete ending, but quality maintained.
Where to Watch

UK: BBC iPlayer

Final Score
Years

Creators
Steven Moffat, Mark Gatiss
What It Feels Like to Watch
Sherlock is what happens when you take Arthur Conan Doyle's detective and drop him into modern London with a smartphone. Benedict Cumberbatch plays Sherlock Holmes as a consulting detective who texts, blogs, and uses nicotine patches instead of a pipe. Martin Freeman is Dr. John Watson, a wounded veteran of Afghanistan who becomes Sherlock's flatmate and chronicler. The game is the same—only the technology has changed.
Steven Moffat and Mark Gatiss created something that felt instantly definitive. The modernization is clever without being gimmicky: Sherlock's deductions appear as on-screen text messages; Watson's blog replaces his published stories; Moriarty operates through criminal networks and digital heists. But at its heart, this is still Holmes and Watson, the brilliant sociopath and the warm-hearted doctor.
The first two seasons are nearly perfect. Each 90-minute episode is a feature film in miniature. "A Scandal in Belgravia" gives us Irene Adler as a dominatrix who outsmarts Sherlock until she doesn't. "The Reichenbach Fall" ends with Sherlock apparently dead and Watson grieving at his grave. The cliffhanger between seasons two and three dominated internet speculation for two years.
Cumberbatch's Sherlock became a cultural phenomenon—the cheekbones, the coat, the rapid-fire deductions delivered with barely contained contempt for lesser minds. But Martin Freeman's Watson is equally important: he humanizes Sherlock, provides the emotional core, and serves as our entry point into a world of genius detectives and impossible crimes.
The ranking is for seasons 1-3 only. Season 4 is widely considered a disappointment—overplotted, self-indulgent, and more interested in teasing future twists than delivering satisfying conclusions. The show that delighted audiences with its cleverness ended by outsmarting itself.

Shetland
2013 - Present • BBC • Ongoing
Score: 7.23
Crime Drama
What It Feels Like
Detective Inspector Jimmy Perez works murders on the Shetland Islands—closer to Norway than Scotland. The islands are beautiful and isolated; the community is close-knit; everyone knows everyone. Douglas Henshall is Perez—quiet, competent, carrying loss. Ann Cleeves' novels adapted into Scottish noir: the landscape is as important as the crimes, and the crimes are always personal.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8/10)
Douglas Henshall's Perez is the Scottish detective tradition extended: dour, dedicated, the quiet man who notices. Alison O'Donnell as Tosh provides the partnership. The supporting cast creates the island community—everyone has history, everyone has secrets. The performances are grounded and authentic.
World Building (9/10)
Shetland: the islands, the sea, the limited daylight, the isolation, the Nordic heritage. The world is specific—this isn't generic Scotland, it's the northernmost islands with their own culture. The landscape is constant; the weather shapes every investigation.
Cinematography (9/10)
The Shetland Islands photographed as character: the cliffs, the sea, the small towns, the long summer light and winter dark. The landscape is majestic and melancholic. BBC Scotland production at its finest.
Visual Spectacle (5/10)
The spectacle is the islands: the landscape, the isolation, the sea. The crimes are personal, not cinematic. The "spectacle" is atmosphere—watching the landscape shape the people who shape the crimes.
Conceptual Density (7/10)
Isolation, community, family secrets, the weight of history, the limits of escape. The islands trap people physically and emotionally. The show explores what happens when everyone knows everyone's business.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Multi-episode mysteries: each case takes 2-4 episodes, allowing the landscape and community to develop. The pacing is deliberate—this is slow-burn crime, not procedural. The drive is understanding what the isolation did to people.
Narrative Path & Resolution (5/10)
Ongoing. The show continues with new lead detective after Henshall's departure. Each story resolves; the series continues. Currently in transition, maintaining the setting and tone.

"The Realm at War"

Year

Rachel Kondo, Justin Marks
What It Feels Like to Watch
Shogun is Game of Thrones without dragons—a political epic set in feudal Japan where the stakes are power, survival, and the soul of a nation. Based on James Clavell's novel, the 2024 adaptation is a prestige production that takes its audience seriously: much of the dialogue is in Japanese with subtitles, the historical detail is meticulous, and the violence is brutal and beautiful.
The year is 1600. The Taiko has died, leaving a young heir and a council of regents. Toranaga (Hiroyuki Sanada) is the most cunning of them, playing a long game while his rivals underestimate him. Into this political intrigue crashes John Blackthorne (Cosmo Jarvis), an English pilot whose ship washes up on Japanese shores. He's the first Englishman most Japanese have seen—a barbarian with knowledge of European tactics and Protestant hatred of Catholic Spain and Portugal.
The show uses Blackthorne as our entry point, but it refuses to make him the hero. He's a useful fool, a pawn in games he doesn't understand. The real story belongs to Toranaga and the Japanese characters navigating a world where honor and deception are indistinguishable. Toda Mariko (Anna Sawai) becomes the heart of the series—a noblewoman trapped between duty and desire, fluent in Portuguese, capable of being Blackthorne's translator and Toranaga's most valuable piece.
The production is cinematic. Battle scenes, castle sieges, sea voyages—it all looks like a feature film expanded across ten hours. The attention to historical detail extends to language, costume, architecture, and the specific codes of bushido that govern every interaction. Characters bow at precise angles; to do so incorrectly is an insult.
This is not a show that explains itself. You learn by watching, by seeing who respects whom and who is plotting against whom. It rewards attention and punishes distraction. The finale is a masterwork of strategic warfare—Toranaga's plan revealed in its full complexity only when it's already too late to stop.

text:
Show Me a Hero
2015 • HBO • 6 Episodes
Score: 7.88
Political Drama, True Story
What It Feels Like
Yonkers, New York, 1987. A federal court orders public housing built in white neighborhoods. The city explodes. Mayor Nick Wasicsko tries to do the right thing and is destroyed for it. The white residents are certain their neighborhoods will be ruined; the Black residents just want decent places to live. David Simon's compassionate camera captures everyone's humanity, even those on the wrong side of history. It's The Wire's moral universe applied to housing policy.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (9/10)
Oscar Isaac as Wasicsko is brilliant—a man who becomes mayor almost by accident, then is destroyed by the act of governing. Catherine Keener, Alfred Molina, Winona Ryder, and Bob Balaban create a complete ecosystem of Yonkers players. The non-professional actors playing residents bring documentary authenticity. Every performance serves the whole. Simon's casting, as always, is immaculate.
World Building (9/10)
Yonkers rendered as microcosm: row houses, project apartments, city council chambers, political backrooms. The city's geography is the conflict—the white neighborhoods, the Black neighborhoods, the demarcation lines. The show teaches while it dramatizes: how housing policy works, how segregation persists, how change happens (or doesn't). Simon's journalism-as-drama approach creates complete worlds.
Cinematography (7/10)
Functional and effective. Simon's shows look like documentaries—unobtrusive camera, natural light, real locations. The style serves the content: this happened, these are the stakes. The housing units themselves become visual motifs: the ones being torn down, the ones being built, the ones people fight to avoid.
Visual Spectacle (3/10)
No spectacle. This is people in rooms, talking, deciding, fighting. The spectacle is the conflict itself: protests, courtroom battles, elections. But the show finds drama in bureaucratic process—how policy becomes reality, how principle faces power. The "spectacle" is procedural intensity.
Conceptual Density (9/10)
Housing segregation as American original sin. The show explores NIMBYism, institutional racism, the difference between personal decency and political courage, the destruction wrought by good intentions facing organized resistance. Wasicsko's arc is about the cost of doing right in a system that punishes it. Simon's most didactic work is also his most morally complex.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
The pace is deliberate—this is David Simon, not Aaron Sorkin. Each episode advances the timeline and the stakes, but momentum builds through understanding rather than acceleration. Audiences seeking thrills will be bored; audiences seeking civic education dramatized will be riveted. The drive is intellectual as much as emotional.
Narrative Path & Resolution (9/10)
A complete miniseries: Wasicsko's rise and fall, the housing built, the resistance fading, the costs tallied. The ending includes the real Wasicsko's fate—a gut-punch that contextualizes everything. Simon knows how to conclude: with truth rather than triumph. Among HBO's finest miniseries.

UK: Amazon Prime Video

"Grief Is Messy"
7.48
Final Score
Years
2023-

Creators
Bill Lawrence, Brett Goldstein, Jason Segel
What It Feels Like to Watch
Shrinking is about what happens when a therapist stops following the rules. Jimmy Laird (Jason Segel) is a grief counselor whose wife died in a car accident. He's not coping. He's drinking, neglecting his daughter, sleeping with clients' mothers. Then he decides to try something new: radical honesty. He tells clients exactly what he thinks. He interferes in their lives. He breaks every ethical guideline.
The show could have been dark—a therapist in freefall. Instead, it's a comedy, and a surprisingly optimistic one. Jimmy's unorthodox approach sometimes works. His clients—Sean (Luke Tennie), an angry veteran; Grace (Heidi Gardner), who can't leave her partner; Alice (Lukita Maxwell), his teenage daughter—start making progress, and Jimmy starts working through his grief.
His colleagues provide contrast and support. Paul (Harrison Ford, in a career-best TV role) is an older therapist with Parkinson's who disapproves of Jimmy's methods but respects his intentions. Gaby (Jessica Williams) is his best friend's widow, complicating everything. Liz (Christa Miller) is the meddling neighbor who inserts herself into every situation.
The show is from Bill Lawrence (Ted Lasso, Scrubs) and Brett Goldstein (Roy Kent himself), and it shares Ted Lasso's belief that messy people trying to help each other is inherently watchable. The grief is real—Jimmy's wife is dead, his daughter is hurting, his best friend is gone. But the show doesn't wallow. Therapy, it suggests, is messy. Recovery is non-linear. And sometimes you need to break the rules to find what works.
Harrison Ford's deadpan delivery as Paul is a running gag that never gets old. "I have Parkinson's. I'm not dying. I'm just going to deteriorate slowly in front of you." His gruffness hides genuine care.

text:
Silo
2023 • Sci-Fi Mystery | 2 Seasons
Score: 8.15
Sci-Fi, Mystery, Dystopian
What It Feels Like to Watch
Silo is a post-apocalyptic mystery about the last ten thousand people on Earth, living in a mile-deep underground silo where the outside world is so toxic that leaving means certain death. Or that's what they're told. Rebecca Ferguson plays Juliette Nichols, an engineer who discovers that the silo's founding documents have been secretly rewritten, and that everything she's been told about their history might be lies.
The show is adapted from Hugh Howey's self-published trilogy, and its strength is in the world-building: a closed ecosystem where generations have never seen sunlight, where power is concentrated among those who control the cameras and the archives, where the central mystery—what's really outside, what happened to the world, who built the silo—propels narrative. The architecture of the structure becomes character: the stairs between levels that serve as class markers, the gardens that produce oxygen, the mechanical that power the generator.
What distinguishes Silo from other dystopian fiction is its patience. The mysteries unfold deliberately; the world is established before it's explained. Juliette is damaged in ways that feel earned—she's lost people she loved, and her grief motivates her investigation. The show's second season expands the scope without losing focus, revealing that the silo is one of many, that the outside world is more complex than initially shown, and that the systems of control run deeper than anyone imagined. This is science fiction built on curiosity and conspiracy.
Why It Ranks Here
Silo earns its ranking through immersive world-building, Rebecca Ferguson's committed performance, and mystery structure that rewards attention. The score reflects a show that established itself as premium sci-fi in its first two seasons.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7.5/10)
Rebecca Ferguson creates a Juliette whose curiosity is both strength and vulnerability. The ensemble builds as the show progresses—Tim Robbins, Common, and others adding depth to the silo's inhabitants. Character motivation is consistently clear even when behavior surprises.
World Building (9/10)
The silo is one of television's most immersive environments—a complete society with its own economy, class system, religion, and history. The details accumulate: the stairs as death sentences for old bodies, the camera surveillance that creates paranoia, the reproductive lottery that controls population. This is science fiction world-building at its best.
Cinematography (7.5/10)
Claustrophobic environments shot to emphasize confinement while creating beauty from industrial materials. The lighting distinguishes the silo's levels—bright upper levels, shadowy depths. Direction serves mystery without showing off.
Visual Spectacle (4/10)
Set design rather than effects—the silo's levels, the camera rooms, the generator's machinery. The spectacle is architectural, creating a space that feels both lived-in and confining. Some exterior shots expand the visual possibilities in later seasons.
Conceptual Depth (7.5/10)
The show explores control through information, class separation through physical architecture, and how belief systems are constructed and maintained. The mystery emerges from these themes—secrecy is structural, systematic, designed.
Narrative Drive (7.5/10)
The mystery structure creates strong momentum—each episode reveals while withholding. The second season complicates without losing clarity. Two seasons establish premise; continuation will determine whether momentum can be sustained across full source material.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
The show is ongoing; mysteries are partially resolved while new ones emerge. The silo's truths are being revealed, but the full story requires completion. Current satisfaction depends on how much unresolved mystery a viewer can tolerate.

Six Feet Under
"Everything ends"
8.35
Final Score
Years
2001-2005
Episodes
63
Network

Creator
Alan Ball
What It Feels Like to Watch
Six Feet Under is about a family that runs a funeral home—and about death, which they seeevery day. Nathaniel Fisher Sr. (Richard Jenkins) dies in the pilot; his widow Ruth (Frances Conroy) and children Nate (Peter Krause), David (Michael C. Hall), and Claire (Lauren Ambrose) inherit the business and the grief. Each episode opens with a death: some expected, some absurd, all inevitable. "Everything ends," Nate says. The show's thesis: accepting mortality is the only way to live.
The Fisher family is dysfunctional. Nate, who fled home, returns and falls for Brenda (Rachel Griffiths), a massage therapist with a troubled family of her own. David is closeted, datingKeith (Mathew St. Patrick), a Black police officer, navigating sexuality and faith. Claire is the rebellious youngest, artist, lost, seeking. Ruth grieves by trying to control everything, then learning she can't. The show's structure: death every week, but the real story is how the living continue. The dead appear as ghosts, projections, conscience—Nate sees his father everywhere. They're notreal. They're not gone either.
The show's genius is making mortality intimate. Death isn't abstract; it's a customer, a body, a family's grief. The Fishers see every kind of death: old age, suicide, accident, murder. And the show asks: what do we do with this knowledge? Nate faces a brain condition that might kill him. Brenda's brother Billy (Jeremy Sisto) is mentally ill, obsessed with her. David is carjacked and traumatized. Claire falls in love and is abandoned. "The only thing I know for sure is that I'm going to die," Nate says. The show's comfort: so is everyone else. That's the connection.
Five seasons, sixty-three episodes, complete. The finale is legendary: a montage showing every character's death, from Nate (already gone) to Ruth to David to Claire, dying old in 2085. "And I will try to fix you," Coldplay plays. It's the most cathartic ending in television history—a show about death that lets you see everyone's ending, and find peace. "Why do we have to die?" a child asks. "To make life important," Nate answers. It was.

text:
Skins UK
What It Feels Like to Watch
Skins is a British teen drama that follows a group of Bristol teenagers through their final years of school, capturing their parties, relationships, family dramas, and various forms of self-destruction with a frankness that made it controversial and influential. The show premiered in 2007 and ran for seven seasons, with each two-season generation focusing on a new cohort of teenagers. The format allowed the show to refresh before its characters aged out of teen drama.
What distinguished Skins from American teen dramas was its aesthetic: rapid editing, stylized sequences, a willingness to show teenage life as teenagers experienced it rather than as adults wanted it depicted. The characters drink, take drugs, have sex, and make catastrophically bad decisions, but the show's judgment is suspended—they're presented as works in progress rather than moral lessons. Some episodes were written by teenagers, contributing to the authenticity that critics found either refreshing or dangerous.
The first generation—Effy, Tony, Jal, Chris, and others—established the show's tone: beautiful, damaged young people hurting each other and themselves in ways that felt genuinely unpredictable. The show's most powerful moments came from its willingness to follow consequences to their logical ends: death, mental illness, the permanent damage that teenage choices can create. It was never a show about teenagers learning valuable lessons; it was about teenagers surviving or not surviving the process of becoming adults.
Why It Ranks Here
Skins earns its ranking through authentic teen perspective, generational refresh format, and willingness to show consequences. The score reflects a show that was influential without being formally innovative.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7/10)
The show launched several careers—Nicholas Hoult, Dev Patel, Kaya Scodelario—and discovered young actors with genuine presence. Each generation creates distinct personalities with authentic teenage energy. The performances are raw in ways that professional adult acting isn't, which serves the material.
World Building (6.5/10)
Bristol teenage life is rendered with attention to how teenagers actually live: parties, drugs, awkward sex, family dysfunction that you can't escape yet. The world feels specific to place and class in ways that American teen dramas often aren't.
Cinematography (7/10)
The show's visual style was distinctive: rapid editing, montage sequences set to contemporary music, a handheld aesthetic that suggested documentary authenticity. The direction elevated teen drama above its conventional visual language.
Visual Spectacle (3/10)
The spectacle is in youth itself—beautiful young people, parties, substance-fueled experiences. There are no effects sequences. The visual pleasure is in watching attractive people in heightened emotional states.
Conceptual Depth (6/10)
The show explores what happens when adults abdicate responsibility for teenagers, how young people create families from friends, the consequences of treating adolescence as preparation for adulthood rather than lived experience. The themes emerge from character rather than lecture.
Narrative Drive (6.5/10)
The generational structure creates natural endpoints—characters graduate, new characters arrive. Individual episodes focus on single characters, creating depth at the cost of overall momentum. The show is more character study than plot engine.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
Each generation ends, but endings vary in satisfaction. Some characters get resolution; others disappear or die in ways that feel arbitrary rather than meaningful. The show's commitment to unpredictability sometimes worked against narrative coherence.

The show explores what happens when adults abdicate responsibility for teenagers, how young people create families from friends, the consequences of treating adolescence as preparation for adulthood rather than lived experience. The themes emerge from character rather than lecture.

The generational structure creates natural endpoints—characters graduate, new characters arrive. Individual episodes focus on single characters, creating depth at the cost of overall momentum. The show is more character study than plot engine.

Each generation ends, but endings vary in satisfaction. Some characters get resolution; others disappear or die in ways that feel arbitrary rather than meaningful. The show's commitment to unpredictability sometimes worked against narrative coherence.

What It Feels Like to Watch
Slow Horses is British spy fiction with a hangover. Slough House is where MI5 sends agents who've failed—spectacularly, embarrassingly, or just inconveniently. They're the "slow horses," maintained on the payroll but kept far from real intelligence work. They file reports, do busywork, and hope for a chance to prove themselves. They're led by Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), a brilliant operative who's let himself become a grotesque—fat, flatulent, alcoholic, deliberately repulsive.
River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) is the hotshot who made a training error that nearly killed civilians. Sid Baker (Olivia Cooke) might be an undercover agentMonitoring the house. Catherine Standish (Saskia Reeves) is the administrator with a drinking problem she's managed. Every slow horse has a story, and half the drama is discovering why each one ended up in purgatory.
Then there's a real case. A kidnapping, a threat, a conspiracy. Regent's Park—MI5's headquarters, led by Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas)—wants to handle it cleanly. The slow horses stumble into it, or are used as assets, and suddenly Jackson Lamb is being Jackson Lamb: brilliant, vicious, loyal to his rejects and absolutely lethal to anyone who threatens them.
Gary Oldman is extraordinary—a performance of controlled chaos, hiding intellect behind slovenly manners. The supporting cast matches him. The tone balances bleak British humor with genuine thriller tension. This isn't Bond; it's the office park where Bond's messes get cleaned up, by the people who made their own messes.
Based on Mick Herron's novels, each season adapts one book. They're standalone stories with continuing character arcs—perfect for the limited-series model Apple TV+ favors.

text:
Small Axe
2020 • BBC/Amazon • 5 Films
Score: 7.80
Anthology, Historical Drama
What It Feels Like
Five films, one community. London's West Indian diaspora from the 1960s to 1980s: the Mangrove restaurant trial, the education system failing Black children, the police harassment, the dance parties that were resistance, the dreams deferred and the dreams achieved. Steve McQueen (the filmmaker, not the actor) creates a cinematic testimony—"small axe" from the proverb: small axe cut down big tree. Each film is complete; together they compose an epic of Black British survival and joy.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (9/10)
Each film features distinct performances: Letitia Wright and Shaun Parkes in "Mangrove," the courtroom drama; John Boyega in "Red, White and Blue" as a man joining the police to change them; Micheal Ward and Amarah-Jae St. Aubyn in "Lovers Rock," the house party as liberation. The casting is precise, the performances uniformly excellent. This is cinema acting in television format.
World Building (9/10)
West London across decades: Notting Hill before gentrification, the front rooms, the blues parties, the police stations, the restaurants. Each film creates a specific time and place with meticulous detail. The world expands across films—characters recur, references cross-pollinate. A community rendered in five facets, each complete, each connected.
Cinematography (9/10)
Steve McQueen is a filmmaker, not a television director. Each film is shot like cinema. "Lovers Rock" alone is worth watching for its house party sequence—light, movement, sound creating something approaching religious experience. The camera work is patient, observant, beautiful. This is visual art.
Visual Spectacle (6/10)
The spectacle varies: courtroom drama in "Mangrove," domestic conflict in "Education," dance floor ecstasy in "Lovers Rock." The spectacle is emotional rather than production-driven. McQueen finds beauty in community spaces, in faces, in movement. Modest budgets, extraordinary vision.
Conceptual Density (9/10)
Each film carries its themes: institutional racism, community resistance, generational conflict, the limits of assimilation, joy as survival strategy. "Small axe" is the central metaphor: a small community can challenge power. The anthology format allows McQueen to explore different angles of diaspora experience. Intellectual without being academic.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Each film is self-contained, so narrative momentum is episodic. "Mangrove" is courtroom procedural; "Lovers Rock" is almost plotless—a party and its aftermath. The drive comes from character and atmosphere rather than plot twists. Patient viewers will be rewarded; action seekers may struggle.
Narrative Path & Resolution (8/10)
Each film provides resolution—trials conclude, parties end, educations transform. The anthology structure means no single ending, but each ending is appropriate. "Red, White and Blue" ends on uncomfortable optimism; "Education" ends with possibility. McQueen resists easy triumph while delivering emotional completion.
Where to Watch
US: Amazon Prime Video
UK: BBC iPlayer, Amazon Prime Video

headings: What It Feels Like to Watch
text:
Smallville
2001 • Superhero Origin • 217 Episodes
Score: 7.02
Drama, Superhero
What It Feels Like to Watch
Smallville reimagined Superman as a teen drama, and in doing so, discovered something fundamental: Clark Kent's adolescence is the most interesting part of his story. Before he can fly, before he works at the Daily Planet, before he becomes the icon—there's just a kid from Kansas with abilities he doesn't understand trying to navigate high school, friendship, and the gradual discovery of who he's meant to be.
Tom Welling plays Clark during his formative years, and the show's genius is in treating the superhero origin as something to be discovered rather than shown. We know he'll become Superman; the pleasure is in watching him not become Superman, episode after episode, as he learns control and responsibility. The kryptonite-of-the-week formula allowed for monster-of-the-week storytelling while developing the central relationships: Clark and Lana, Clark and Chloe, and especially Clark and Lex Luthor.
Smallville is a show that defined the CW aesthetic for a decade—glossy, emotional, serialized in ways that network television hadn't fully embraced for genre shows. Its production values date it, and its ten-season run extended past its natural endpoint, but at its peak it was a genuinely innovative approach to superhero storytelling. It proved that you could strip away the costume and the iconography and still have compelling television. Every modern superhero origin story owes something to what Smallville attempted and often achieved.
Why It Ranks Here
Smallville earns its ranking for defining the superhero-origin-as-teen-drama template, for its central Clark-Lex relationship, and for a run that maintained quality past the point where most network shows decline. The score reflects its influence and its peaks.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7/10)
Welling grows into the role over ten seasons, starting as a convincingly awkward teenager and ending as someone approaching heroic weight. Michael Rosenbaum's Lex Luthor is the show's secret weapon—their friendship and its deterioration is more compelling than any of the weekly villains. Kristin Kreuk and Allison Mack create memorable female characters in a genre that often forgets them.
World Building (7/10)
Smallville, Kansas becomes a character—a place of secrets, kryptonite, and meteor freaks. The show built its own mythology while connecting to Superman lore in ways that rewarded longtime fans. The origin elements—discovering powers, finding the fortress, learning about Krypton—were paced effectively across seasons.
Cinematography (6/10)
Early 2000s television aesthetics: bright lighting, attractive casts, composition that serves story without style. The show looks like its era, which hasn't aged particularly well. The visual effects improved over the run but never reached film quality. The direction is functional rather than distinctive.
Visual Spectacle (5/10)
The spectacle is in powers discovered—super speed, heat vision, the gradual development of abilities. But television budgets limited what could be shown, and Smallville relied more on character drama than action spectacle. The occasional flying sequences in later seasons were notable for finally happening.
Conceptual Depth (6/10)
The show genuinely explored what it would mean to grow up with abilities you couldn't control, to be different in a small town, to have to hide who you are. The Clark-Lex relationship is the most interesting: watching a good man become a villain through choices that feel inevitable only in retrospect.
Narrative Drive (6.5/10)
The monster-of-the-week structure provided reliable episode arcs while the serialized elements—Clark's powers, Lex's descent, the mythological revelations—developed over seasons. Ten seasons is too long; the show repeated itself past natural conclusions. But at its peak, it balanced episodic and serialized storytelling well.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
The finale delivered what fans wanted—Clark puts on the suit, becomes Superman—but the journey to that endpoint meandered through seasons of filler. The show found its natural ending several times and kept going. The final episodes honor what came before without matching the peak.

text:
Snowdrop
2021 - 2022 • JTBC • 16 Episodes
Score: 7.15
Romance, Historical
What It Feels Like
1987 Seoul. A university student finds a wounded young man in her dormitory. She hides him, nurses him, falls in love with him. He's a North Korean spy. She doesn't know. Jung Hae-in and Jisoo (from BLACKPINK) star in the Korean historical romance: democracy protests as backdrop, forbidden love as engine. Tragedy is foreshadowed from the first frame.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8/10)
Jung Hae-in as Soo-ho: the North Korean agent who didn't choose this life. Jisoo as Young-ro: the student whose heart overcomes her fear. The chemistry carries the tragedy. The supporting cast creates the political context.
World Building (9/10)
1987 South Korea: the democracy protests, the spy networks, the university dormitories, the divided Korea. The world is specific and researched—the political tension is as real as the romance.
Cinematography (8/10)
K-drama production: Seoul's winter rendered beautifully, the dormitory hiding the spy, the protests filling the streets. The style is romantic—the snow, the longing looks, the impending tragedy.
Visual Spectacle (4/10)
The spectacle is emotional: the protests, the confrontation, the inevitable tragedy. This is romance against history—not action, but feeling. The production value serves the emotion.
Conceptual Density (8/10)
Love across political divides, the individual vs. the state, whether we can escape our origins, democracy's cost. The show explores Korean history through a love story that cannot end well.
Narrative Drive (8/10)
The clock is ticking: Soo-ho must escape; Young-ro must hide him; the spies are hunting. The structure is countdown—each episode brings the danger closer. The foreshadowing creates dread.
Narrative Path & Resolution (8/10)
Complete. The tragedy is delivered as promised. The ending is devastating but earned. Korean drama at its most affecting.

UK: Disney+

"Ride Free or Die"

Final Score

What It Feels Like to Watch
Sons of Anarchy is Shakespeare in a leather cut. Kurt Sutter took Hamlet, set it in an MC, and somehow made it work for seven seasons. Jax Teller is the prince; Clay the usurping uncle; Gemma the scheming mother. The motorcycles are incidental to the tragedy.
The show's greatest strength is also its weakness: it never stops escalating. Every season must top the last in violence, betrayal, and body count. Characters die brutally, loyalties shift constantly, and by the end you're exhausted. But you can't look away. Charlie Hunnam's Jax transforms from idealist to monster before your eyes, and you understand every step of his descent.
The supporting cast is phenomenal. Katey Sagal's Gemma is one of television's great villains—manipulative, terrifying, yet somehow sympathetic. Ron Perlman's Clay is Shakespearean in his ambition and downfall. The club itself becomes a character, with its own codes and contradictions.

Characters & Acting (8.5): Jax, Gemma, Clay, Tig, Juice—these are indelible characters. The club dynamics feel authentic. Katey Sagal deserved every award for her portrayal of a mother whose love is indistinguishable from toxicity.
Narrative Drive (9): This show never slows down. Every episode ends with a cliffhanger, a death, or a betrayal. It's pure adrenaline. The problem is sustainability—by season 6, the escalation feels forced.
Resolution (8): The finale is perfect. Jax goes out on his own terms, in a callback to his father's death, riding into the sunset (and a truck). The circular tragedy completes itself.
Key Episodes
"J'ai Obtenu Cette" (S2E13) — The season 2 finale. The Irish, the ATF, the club falling apart—and somehow pulling together. Peak SOA.
"Laying Pipe" (S5E3) — Opie's death in prison. The single most devastating moment in the series. "I got this."
"Papa's Goods" (S7E13) — The series finale. Jax's suicide ride is Shakespearean tragedy at its finest. The final montage is perfect.

What It Feels Like to Watch
Southland is a cop show without the safety net. No procedurals, no easy resolutions, no clear heroes and villains. It follows patrol officers and detectives through Los Angeles, a city portrayed with documentary authenticity—gritty, desperate, beautiful. The show has more in common with The Wire than Law & Order.
Officer John Cooper (Michael Cudlitz) is the veteran training Officer Ben Sherman (Ben McKenzie), a rookie whose idealism gets tested every shift. Cooper is gay, closeted at work, dealing with back pain that threatens his career. His cruelty to Sherman early on gives way to something like respect, even friendship.
Officer Lydia Adams (Regina King) is the best detective in the precinct—smart, relentless, dealing with suspects and victims with equal intensity. Her partner rotations become a running thread: nobody can keep up with her, and some partners can't handle the job at all.
Officer Sammy Bryant (Shawn Hatosy) and his partner "Nate" Moretta (Kevin Alejandro) patrol the gang units, dealing with informants, vendettas, and violence that bleeds into their personal lives. When something devastating happens to Nate, Sammy's grief becomes the sharpest story the show ever tells.
The handheld camera style creates immediacy. The dialogue overlaps. The cases don't resolve neatly. The show understands that police work is mostly boredom interrupted by terror, that LA is a city of contradictions, and that everyone on the force is one bad day away from breaking.

text:
Spiral (Engrenages)
2005 - 2020 • Canal+ • 86 Episodes
Score: 7.60
Crime, Legal Drama, Thriller
What It Feels Like
The France tourists never see. Housing projects, police stations, courtrooms where justice is negotiated rather than delivered. A legal system that operates on deals and blackmail as much as evidence. Women in power—judges, lawyers, captains—fighting through institutions designed for men. It's The Wire if The Wire were French and focused on the intersection of policing and prosecution. Paris looks like what it is: beautiful and savage in equal measure.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8/10)
Caroline Proust as Captain Laure Berthaud is one of television's great detectives—compulsive, brilliant, self-destructive, maternal toward her team and no one else. Grégory Fitoussi's prosecutor Pierre Clément is the moral center that erodes season by season. Thierry Godard as Gilou is the loyal fuckup who breaks your heart. The ensemble is deep, French-trained actors bringing theatrical intensity to genre television.
World Building (8/10)
The French legal system rendered comprehensible to outsiders: juges d'instruction (investigating judges), procureurs (prosecutors), avocats (defense attorneys), and the police who navigate between them. The banlieues, the courtrooms, the prisons—each location has its own rules, its own economy. This is institutional television that teaches while it entertains.
Cinematography (6/10)
Canal+ budget means it looks better than American broadcast but short of HBO prestige. The Paris that appears is gray, institutional, lived-in. The style is functional—serving story rather than calling attention to itself. Night scenes in the projects have genuine danger; courtroom scenes have procedural clarity. Effective, not spectacular.
Visual Spectacle (5/10)
This isn't spectacle TV. The spectacle is in the system revealed: how French justice actually functions, how power flows through institutions. The visuals serve the revelation, not the reverse. When violence occurs, it's shocking precisely because the show isn't about violence—it's about the machinery of justice that violence feeds.
Conceptual Density (8/10)
The French system of investigating judges is unique—magistrates who both investigate and judge, creating conflicts of interest built into the system. Spiral explores institutional corruption not as exception but as norm. The law is not a refuge but a battlefield. These are sophisticated ideas delivered through propulsive storytelling.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Season-long cases with weekly complications. The structure is The Wire—a single investigation unfolding across episodes. But Spiral is less patient, accelerating toward resolutions that sometimes feel unearned. The momentum is strong but occasionally sacrifices depth for closure. Still, each season is designed to be consumed, and consume you it will.
Narrative Path & Resolution (8/10)
Eight seasons with a planned conclusion. The final season brings everything full circle—careers ending, institutions continuing, personal costs finally tallied. The show understands that in police work, there are no victories, only survivors. The resolution honors that truth. Main characters die, retire, or continue broken. It's honest about the cost of the job.

text:
Sports Night
1998 • ABC • 45 Episodes
Score: 6.95
Comedy, Drama, Workplace
What It Feels Like
Behind the scenes at CSC, a cable sports network, where a team produces a nightly sports show. Aaron Sorkin's first television series—before The West Wing, before The Newsroom—shows his signature emerging: walk-and-talks, rapid dialogue, workplace-as-family, idealists fighting corporate compromise. Peter Krause plays anchor Casey McCall, trying to be professional while divorced and middle-aged; Josh Charles plays Dan Rydell, recovering from depression; Felicity Huffman is executive producer Dana Whitaker, competent and overwhelmed. The show aired on ABC with laugh track and studio audience; Sorkin fought both. The studio won. Watch it without the laugh track and you see the drama Sorkin intended. It's funny—genuinely—but it's not a sitcom. It's about people who love their work and each other, failing upward at a job that will consume them.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8.5/10)
Peter Krause and Josh Charles have chemistry that reads as years of friendship. Felicity Huffman's Dana is the show's emotional center—competent, insecure, trying to run a show and a life. Sabrina Lloyd's Natalie and Josh Malina's Jeremy provide romantic subplot. Robert Guillaume's Isaac Jaffe is the professional father figure. The cast makes Sorkin's dialogue sing.
World Building (7/10)
The CSC network is corporate bureaucracy; the show-within-a-show is chaotic professionalism. 1990s cable television feels authentic (because it was close to Sorkin's experience). The sports world is present but secondary—the show is about production, not athletics.
Cinematography (6.5/10)
Multi-camera sitcom style with Sorkin's evolving ambition. The walk-and-talk becomes signature. The show is blocked for comedy timing that doesn't match the dramatic content. The Sorkin style—visible in later work—struggles with network notes.
Visual Spectacle (2/10)
None. Studio sets, production monitors, office furniture. The spectacle is rapid dialogue and emotional honesty. This is theater filmed for television.
Conceptual Density (7/10)
Artistic integrity versus commercial pressure. Sorkin's themes—idealism, competence, work as identity—are present but simpler than later work. The workplace-as-family dynamic is warm without being false. The struggle to produce something good in impossible conditions is Sorkin's autobiography.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Show production provides weekly structure; relationship arcs provide emotional continuity. Sorkin writes weekly without planning—sometimes brilliant, sometimes filler. Casey-Dana unresolved tension keeps momentum. The show fights format and wins occasionally.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
Cancelled after two seasons. The finale addresses cancellation by having the show within the show face cancellation. Casey and Dana finally get together. Isaac faces health issues. Sorkin moved to The West Wing; the cast dispersed. The ending is premature but not incomplete.

Squid Game
"Red light, green light"
8.10
Final Score
Years
2021-
Episodes
9
Network
Netflix
Creator
Hwang Dong-hyuk
What It Feels Like to Watch
Squid Game is about desperation disguised as childhood. 456 people, deeply in debt, are invited to play children's games for money. "Red light, green light" is the first: move on green, freeze on red, die if you move. The winner takes ₩45.6 billion. Everyone else dies. The show's premise is Battle Royale meets Parasite—a critique of capitalism so sharp it drew global attention. It became Netflix's most-watched series ever.
Seong Gi-hun (Lee Jung-jae) is a gambling addict who lives with his mother, barely sees his daughter, and is broke beyond hope. He joins the game for money. Cho Sang-woo (Park Hae-soo) is his childhood friend, a former investment banker disgraced by embezzlement. Kang Sae-byeok (Jung Ho-yeon) is a North Korean defector trying to get her mother out and her brother to safety. Oh Il-nam (O Yeong-su) is an old man with a brain tumor who wants to play before he dies. They become allies, then rivals, then victims.
The games are simple: tug of war, marbles, the titular squid game. The horror is watching people kill each other for money—watching friendships form and break, watching humanity stripped away game by game. The twist: the old man (Il-nam) created the games. He's a billionaire who was bored. He wanted to play. He faked his death in the first round. The show's thesis: the rich treat the poor as entertainment. Capitalism is a game rigged for those who already won.
One season, nine episodes, season two coming. Squid Game is a phenomenon—not just for its violence, but for its clarity. It says what many feel: the system is broken, the poor are desperate, the rich are cruel. "You're all the same," Gi-hun tells the organizers. They are. He wins. He loses everyone he cared about. He doesn't spend the money. He can't. He's broken. Season two is promised. But the first season said everything it needed to say.

text:
Star Trek: Strange New Worlds
2022 - Present • Paramount+ • Ongoing
Score: 7.18
Sci-Fi, Adventure
What It Feels Like
Christopher Pike commands the USS Enterprise before Kirk. Spock is his science officer. Uhura is a cadet. The show returns to Trek's original format: episodic adventures, moral dilemmas, optimism. Anson Mount is Pike: the captain who knows his future but leads anyway. Classic Trek for the streaming era.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (9/10)
Anson Mount's Pike is among Trek's best captains: warm, authoritative, human. Ethan Peck as Spock honors Nimoy while making the role his own. Rebecca Romijn as Number One, Celia Rose Gooding as Uhura, Babs Olusanmokun as M'Benga—the ensemble captures the Trek spirit.
World Building (9/10)
The Federation, the Enterprise, the final frontier: the show returns to Gene Roddenberry's vision with modern production. The worlds visited each episode feel distinct. The optimistic future is restored.
Cinematography (8/10)
Paramount+ production: the Enterprise rendered with detail, alien worlds designed with care, space photographed beautifully. The style honors the original while updating the effects. Classic Trek aesthetics, modern budget.
Visual Spectacle (8/10)
Alien planets, space battles, new civilizations. The spectacle is classic Trek: the ship, the shuttles, the strange new worlds. Each episode delivers visual wonder alongside moral questions.
Conceptual Density (8/10)
Pike's foreknowledge of his death, Spock's human-Vulcan dual nature, the Prime Directive, diplomacy vs. intervention. The show explores classic Trek themes: optimism, moral complexity, the better angels of our nature.
Narrative Drive (8/10)
Episodic adventures with serialized character development. Each episode is a complete story—the format fans wanted. The Pike arc (knowing his future) provides ongoing tension. The drive is exploration itself.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
Ongoing. Three seasons completed or in production. The show knows its endpoint (Pike's fate is established in Trek canon) but hasn't reached it. Currently successful and acclaimed.

text:
Station Eleven
2021 • HBO Max • 10 Episodes
Score: 7.45
Dystopian, Drama
What It Feels Like
A flu pandemic wipes out civilization. A traveling symphony performs Shakespeare in the ruins. Before the collapse, an actor dies on stage; after, his connections—ex-wife, audience member, the child who witnessed—navigate a world where art still matters. Emily St. John Mandel's novel adapted into television that's less about apocalypse than about what survives. "Survival is insufficient."
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8/10)
Mackenzie Davis as Kirsten, the actress who survives; Himesh Patel as Jeevan, the reluctant protector; Danielle Deadwyler as Miranda, the woman who wrote the comic that gives the show its title. The performances are understated, internal. The child actors (Matilda Lawler as young Kirsten) are remarkable. Everyone carries grief quietly.
World Building (8/10)
Post-apocalyptic Michigan: the abandoned airport, the settlements, the roads where danger lurks. The pre-pandemic world is rendered as precious memory. The Symphony's travels create geography: what's been lost, what remains. The world is sad and beautiful.
Cinematography (8/10)
HBO production: the pandemic is sudden, the collapse is quiet, the aftermath is visually poetic. The show finds beauty in ruin—sunsets over empty highways, stages in abandoned buildings. The visual language is mournful without being grim.
Visual Spectacle (4/10)
The spectacle is absence: empty cities, abandoned homes, the quiet of a world with fewer people. The "spectacle" is emotional—art continuing after everything ends. Subtle beauty rather than blockbuster apocalypse.
Conceptual Density (9/10)
Art as survival, memory as resistance, the connections between strangers. The show explores what makes life worth living when civilization ends—theater, music, stories, the comic book that connects characters across time. Philosophical without being academic. "Survival is insufficient" as organizing principle.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
The show jumps in time: before the pandemic, the early days, twenty years after. The structure is puzzle-box—connections emerge slowly. The drive is understanding: how do these people connect? What happened to whom? Patient viewers rewarded.
Narrative Path & Resolution (9/10)
Complete miniseries. All threads connect; the comic's significance is revealed; the final episode brings characters together across time and distance. The ending is hopeful without being sentimental. Appropriate, beautiful, finished.

What It Feels Like
Megan is a suburban mom with a past. Ray is a photographer who can't escape his. Broome is a detective obsessed with a missing persons case. Their stories intertwine when the past returns. Harlan Coben adaptation: secrets, lies, and the danger of buried truths.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7/10)
Cush Jumbo as Megan, James Nesbitt as Ray, Richard Armitage as Broome. The ensemble creates the web of secrets. The performances are thriller-competent—everyone has something to hide.
World Building (7/10)
Suburban Atlantic City: the comfortable life, the strip clubs of the past, the missing persons who connect them. The world is noir hidden in suburbia—two Americas, one visible, one buried.
Cinematography (6/10)
Netflix Coben production: suburbia and strip clubs, past and present, the contrast between who they were and who they are now. The style is thriller standard.

What It Feels Like to Watch
Stranger Things is a love letter to 1980s America. Hawkins, Indiana, is a small town where kids ride bikes, play Dungeons & Dragons, and worry about girls. Then Will Byers disappears. His mother Joyce (Winona Ryder) believes he's in the walls, speaking through Christmas lights. His friends—Mike, Dustin, Lucas—find a girl with a shaved head and telekinetic powers. She's called Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown). She escaped from a government lab. And something else came with her.
The show merges Stephen King, Steven Spielberg, and John Carpenter: kids on bikes facing cosmic horror, government conspiracies, and alternate dimensions. The Upside Down is a dark mirror of our world—cold, decaying, filled with monsters. The Demogorgon hunts. The Mind Flayer spreads. Eleven is the weapon—and the victim. "Friends don't lie," she learns. She's been lied to her whole life. Now she has people who tell her the truth.
Season one is perfect: the mystery, the bond between the kids, Hopper (David Harbour) as the broken sheriff who finds purpose. Season two expands the world—the lab's history, Eleven's "sister," the tunnels beneath Hawkins. Season three is summer: the mall, puberty, the Mind Flayer possessing townspeople. Season four splits the globe—Russia, California, Hawkins—and introduces Vecna, the most terrifying villain yet. The show's strength is its characters: the kids grow up, the adults struggle, the monsters evolve.
Four seasons, thirty-four episodes, final season coming. Stranger Things is Netflix's biggest hit—the show that proved streaming could create cultural phenomena. It's nostalgia as weapon: every reference, every song, every aesthetic choice says "remember this?" But beneath the references is a story about trauma, about finding family, about kids who face horror and refuse to break. "She's our friend and she's crazy," Dustin says of Eleven. She is. That's why they love her.

Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip
2006 - 2007 • NBC • 22 Episodes
Score: 7.33
Drama, Workplace
What It Feels Like
Matt Albie and Danny Tripp are hired to save a failing sketch comedy show. They're brilliant writers; they're also damaged. Amanda Peet is the network executive who believes in them. Aaron Sorkin takes his West Wing formula behind the scenes at Saturday Night Live—walk-and-talk dialogue, workplace romance, crisis-of-the-week television. The show that launched the same year as 30 Rock, was expected to dominate, and was cancelled after one season.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (8/10)
Matthew Perry as Matt is Sorkin's voice: the brilliant writer with anxiety and drug problems. Bradley Whitford as Danny is the producer who loves the wrong woman. Amanda Peet as Jordan brings authority and warmth. The ensemble (Steven Weber, Sarah Paulson, D.L. Hughley) is Sorkin-perfect. Perry's performance is underrated.
World Building (9/10)
Behind the scenes at Saturday Night Live: the writers' room, the stage, the control room, the network offices. The sketch-show infrastructure is rendered with Sorkin's usual accuracy. The world is complete—you understand how the show works.
Cinematography (7/10)
Sorkin walk-and-talk: steadicam following characters through halls, dialogue delivered at speed. The style is familiar from West Wing, adapted to entertainment. The backstage world looks lived-in and professional.
Visual Spectacle (3/10)
No spectacle. This is people making television: meetings, rehearsals, drafts. The sketches themselves are rarely shown; the focus is the process, not the product. Workplace drama without action.
Conceptual Density (7/10)
Art vs. commerce, network censorship, faith and doubt, love and addiction. Sorkin's themes are present: can good television survive? Can damaged people produce great work? The show is earnest in ways that dated it.
Narrative Drive (8/10)
Episode-by-episode: the show must go on, a sketch is problematic, an actor has a crisis. The serialized arcs involve Matt and Harriet's relationship, Danny and Jordan's relationship, the network's survival. The pacing is Sorkin-fast; the drive is constant.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6/10)
One season, cancelled. The finale provides closure for the relationships, but the show was cancelled before it could develop. The cancellation wasn't about quality—30 Rock won the sketch-comedy-show-behind-the-scenes competition. A victim of timing.

What It Feels Like to Watch
Succession is King Lear with private jets. Logan Roy (Brian Cox) is the founder and CEO of Waystar Royco, a media conglomerate worth billions. He's eighty, having health problems, and his four children are circling. Kendall (Jeremy Strong) wants to succeed his father—and has been publicly denied. Shiv (Sarah Snook) is a political consultant who thinks she deserves the throne. Roman (Kieran Culkin) is the vulgarian, a chaos agent who might be smarter than he pretends. Connor (Alan Ruck) is the eldest, the ignored, the fool running for president.
The show's genius is making billionaires sympathetic—or at least understandable. These are horrible people: Logan destroys anyone who crosses him; Kendall enables a waiter's death and covers it up; Shiv betrays her husband for corporate power; Roman makes jokes about children. But they're also family: Logan, dying, asks his children to come. Kendall, destroyed by his father, still wants his approval. "He's a monster," Shiv says about her father. "He's our monster." They can't escape. They don't want to. They just want to win.
The dialogue is Shakespearean profanity—insults as art, cruelty as love language. "You're not serious people," Logan tells his children. He's right. They're not. They're grown adults with billion-dollar trust funds, fighting for a father who will never love them enough. The show's thesis: wealth doesn't make people evil; it reveals what they already were. These people were broken before the money. The money just bought them jets to crash in.
Four seasons, thirty-nine episodes, complete. The finale is devastating: Kendall doesn't get the company. Shiv votes against him. Tom (Matthew Macfadyen), the husband she never loved, becomes CEO. Roman walks away broken. Logan dies mid-season, and his children scatter. "Who is the number one boy?" Logan once asked Kendall. In the end, no one is. Logan's chair is empty. His children stare at the water.

text:
Superman & Lois
2021 • Superhero Drama • 53 Episodes
Score: 7.18
Action, Drama, Superhero
What It Feels Like to Watch
Superman & Lois is what happens when someone realizes that the most interesting thing about Superman isn't his powers—it's his marriage. The show moves Clark and Lois from Metropolis to Smallville, where they're raising teenage twins and navigating the particular challenges of parenting when one parent is the most powerful being on Earth and the other is one of its most driven journalists.
Tyler Hoechlin plays Superman with a warmth that makes the character likeable rather than boring—his Clark is genuinely good, genuinely in love with Lois, genuinely trying to be a father while saving the world. Elizabeth Tulloch's Lois has the drive and intelligence that makes her a believable partner rather than a damsel. The twins—one developing powers, one not—create family drama that grounds the superhero action in real stakes: what happens when you can't save everyone, when your children face dangers you can't punch away.
The show's genius is in its scale. Smallville-sized conflicts—high school football, mortgage payments, family secrets—coexist with world-ending threats, and the show treats both as serious. The action sequences are better than most television superhero work, but the show earns its ranking through the family dynamics. This is a Superman who's tired, a Lois who's torn between career and family, teenagers who are making mistakes that matter. The CW's production constraints show in places, but the storytelling compensates.
Why It Ranks Here
Superman & Lois earns its ranking through a fresh approach to a well-worn character, committed performances, and family drama that makes the superhero elements matter. The score reflects a show that understands Superman is more interesting when he has something to lose.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7.5/10)
Hoechlin and Tulloch create a marriage that serves as the show's emotional engine. The teen actors bring distinct personalities to the twins—one angsty, one anxious—and the family dynamics feel genuine. The villains are variable, but the core cast is consistently strong.
World Building (7/10)
Smallville is rendered with attention to economic decline, high school dynamics, and the particular texture of small-town life. The show grounds Superman in a specific place rather than floating him above a generic city. The superhero elements integrate without overwhelming the setting.
Cinematography (7/10)
The action sequences are staged with clarity and impact that exceeds typical television superhero work. The flight scenes are convincing, the fights have weight. The small-town setting is shot with warmth that matches the family focus.
Visual Spectacle (7/10)
For television, the effects work is impressive. Superman's powers are visualized effectively—flight, strength, heat vision all look good. The spectacle serves story rather than overwhelming it. The show understands that a well-executed rescue matters more than a flashy fight.
Conceptual Depth (6.5/10)
The show engages with questions about parenting, responsibility, and what it means to protect people who need to make their own mistakes. Clark's struggle to be present for his family while saving the world is a genuine tension, not just plot.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
Each episode advances both family drama and superhero plot, with arcs that build across seasons. The teenage storylines provide ongoing tension while the villain of the season provides stakes. The show maintains momentum across seasons without repetitive reset.
Narrative Path & Resolution (6.5/10)
Season finales provide genuine consequence while setting up next seasons. The show doesn't reset between years; things that happened matter going forward. Some resolutions require accepting comic-book logic, but the family dynamics earn their emotional beats.

text:
Surface
2022 • Psychological Thriller • 8 Episodes
Score: 6.68
Thriller, Drama
What It Feels Like to Watch
Surface is a psychological thriller about a woman who survives a suicide attempt—maybe—only to discover that her memory of the event, and everything else, is unreliable. Sophie has lost her recent past; what remains is a life reconstructed from other people's accounts: a wealthy husband, a successful career, a social circle that may or may not have her best interests at heart. The show's central question becomes whether the person she's told she was is the person she wants to be.
The series operates in the tradition of gaslight thrillers—The Girl on the Train, Before I Go to Sleep, any number of stories where a woman's perception of reality is systematically undermined. Gugu Mbatha-Raw carries the material with a performance that conveys Sophie's uncertainty without making her passive; she's investigating her own life, uncovering contradictions in the narratives she's been fed. The show maintains tension effectively through its eight episodes, doling out revelations at a pace designed to maximize uncertainty.
Where Surface falters is in its resolution. The finale reveals come via techniques that feel earned only partially—the explanations for what really happened depend on coincidences and character choices that are hard to reconcile with what we've seen. The show's interest in memory and identity gives way to more conventional thriller mechanics, and the psychological depth it promised in early episodes doesn't quite materialize. It's a well-made genre piece that doesn't transcend its genre, elevated by a lead performance that deserves a more ambitious script.
Why It Ranks Here
Surface earns its position through atmosphere and performance, losing ground on narrative resolution. The psychological thriller elements work while they remain unresolved; the satisfaction diminishes when answers arrive that feel constructed rather than inevitable. The score reflects a competent genre exercise with a standout lead performance.
The 7-Dimension Analysis
Characters & Acting (7/10)
Gugu Mbatha-Raw carries the show with a performance that navigates Sophie's uncertainty without becoming directionless. The character's gradual reassembly of self is conveyed through acting choices—hesitations, reassessments, moments when previous certainties become doubtful. The supporting cast plays characters whose trustworthiness fluctuates, and the performances maintain ambiguity effectively.
World Building (6.5/10)
Surface creates a specific vision of San Francisco wealth—the kind of money that creates comfortable cages, where beautiful spaces can become prisons. The world of Sophie's life is rendered with the appropriate sheen and the appropriate sense of something wrong beneath the surface. The setting serves the themes of class and control without being extensively developed.
Cinematography (7/10)
The visual approach emphasizes memory and unreliability—subjective camera angles, shots that may or may not represent Sophie's perspective, a color palette that subtly shifts based on her emotional state. The direction creates unease without calling attention to itself, building tension through framing and movement rather than effects.
Visual Spectacle (3/10)
This is interior drama, visualized through faces and spaces rather than spectacle. There are no set pieces, no effects, no action sequences that would qualify as spectacle. The visual interest comes entirely from the psychological content, not from anything the show builds or destroys.
Conceptual Depth (6.5/10)
The show raises questions about memory, identity, and whether we can truly know ourselves. Sophie's condition—unable to form new memories reliably—becomes a vehicle for exploring how much of ourselves is constructed from others' accounts. These themes are present throughout but recede in the finale, which prioritizes plot resolution over philosophical engagement.
Narrative Drive (7/10)
The eight-episode structure keeps momentum—each episode reveals something that changes Sophie's understanding, and the audience shares her uncertainty about who to trust. The pacing is deliberate but not slow; the show knows how to withhold information without frustrating. The questions are genuinely engaging while they remain questions.
Narrative Path & Resolution (5.5/10)
The finale provides answers, but they feel less satisfying than the mystery did. Explanations require accepting character behavior that doesn't quite mesh with earlier episodes, and the final twists arrive via contrivance. The resolution works on a plot level—what happened is explained—but doesn't deliver the emotional or thematic payoff the setup promised.
